data.name: Chain_Title
data.value: How a chain works

data.name: Chain_Intro
data.value:
ChainRenamer renames files with a **chain** of small steps. Each step does one simple thing (sort, replace a text…) and works on the result of the step above it, like an assembly line.
The first step is always the **Source**: the folder and the files to rename. Add the next steps with **+ Add a module**; the same module can be used several times. Drag a step by its handle ≡ to change the order: the result changes with it, since each step starts from what the previous one produced.
**Click a step to see what it does.** The grid then shows each name before and after this step, and the names it changes are highlighted. The last step shows the final names. A rule that goes wrong is spotted at once, at the step where it happens.
**Nothing touches the disk** until you click **Apply renaming**. Until then, try anything.
A step can be switched off: it then passes its input on unchanged, which lets you compare with and without it. A step whose settings are not valid (a regular expression being typed, for instance) is marked ⚠ and also passes its input on.
Give a step a name (“Dots to spaces”) to find your way in a long chain: it is shown under its module in the chain.

data.name: Selection_Title
data.value: Check boxes and selection

data.name: Selection_Intro
data.value:
The first column of the grid holds check boxes. They mean two different things, depending on the selected step:
• In the **Source** step, a file left unchecked is **out of the whole chain**. No step sees it, and it is never renamed. • In a step that changes names (Replace…), a file left unchecked is **skipped by this step only**. The step leaves its name as it is, shown in grey italics, and the other steps still work on it. Handy when a rule suits every file but a few.
A Sort step has no check boxes: its column holds the handles ≡ that move the files by hand.
**Fast selection** • The check box in the header checks or unchecks every file. • Shift + click on a check box: the whole range since the last one clicked. • Press on a row and drag: a rectangle selects the rows, as in the Explorer. With Ctrl, they are added to the selection. • Space checks or unchecks the selected rows. A right click offers check, uncheck and invert.

data.name: Apply_Title
data.value: Applying and undoing

data.name: Apply_Intro
Library_Title
data.value: Saved chains and favorites

data.name: Library_Intro
data.value:
A chain is a recipe: **File > Save** keeps its steps and their settings in the library, to replay them later on another folder. The source folder is not saved with it: load the folder, then open the chain from the **Chains** menu.
• **Save** (Ctrl+S) replaces the open chain. **Save as…** (Ctrl+Shift+S) makes a new one, to start from an existing chain. The name is typed in the top bar. • A **•** in the window title means changes not saved yet. Opening another chain or closing the window asks first. • The files unchecked in a step and an order set by hand depend on the loaded files: they are not saved.
**Favorites**, as in a browser: **Chains > In favorites** (Ctrl+D) puts the open chain at the top of the Chains menu. **Organize favorites…** sorts them into folders, which become submenus (Series ▸ Anime). A favorite is only a shortcut: removing it never deletes the chain.
**The library** is a folder holding one `.chain` file per chain, by default `%APPDATA%\ChainRenamer\chains`. **Change the library location…** moves it, to a NAS or a synced folder for example: your chains then follow you from one PC to another.
**Import and export.** **Export this chain…** makes a file to send to someone. **Export the whole library…** makes a zip, for a backup or a new PC. **Import…** takes `.chain` files and these zips; a name already taken gets a number: “Series (2)”.

data.name: Source_Intro
data.value:
The fixed first step: it chooses the files to rename. It cannot be moved nor removed.
Type a folder or click **Browse…**, then **Load**. Local folders and network shares both work, and a slow network does not freeze the window.
Then uncheck the files to leave out: they leave the whole chain (see “Check boxes and selection”). The folder is not saved with the chain: a chain can be replayed on any folder.

data.value: A local folder (`D:\Videos`) or a network share (`\\nas\video\Series`).

data.name: Source_Subfolders_Text
data.value: Also lists the files of every subfolder. Each file stays in its own folder when it is renamed.

data.name: Sort_Intro
data.value:
Puts the files in order. The order matters for the modules that number the files or give them the lines of a list: the first file gets number 1, or the first line.
**Natural order**: the numbers in the names are compared as numbers, so `Episode 2` comes before `Episode 10`. A plain alphabetical sort would put `Episode 10` first.
**By hand**: drag a file by its handle ≡ in the grid. The order set by hand lasts as long as the files stay loaded; it is not saved with the chain. **Back to natural order** cancels it.

data.name: Sort_Descending_Text
data.value: From the last to the first: Z to A, 10 to 1.

data.name: Sort_Example_Natural
data.value: Natural order: 2 before 10

data.name: Sort_Example_Descending
data.value: Descending order

data.name: Replace_Intro
data.value:
Replaces a text by another in the name. The text is searched exactly as it is typed: `.` is a dot. To find a pattern (any number, any word…), use **Replace (advanced)**.
The extension is never touched: replacing `.` by a space keeps `.mkv`.

data.name: Regex_Intro
data.value:
Replaces what a **regular expression** finds: a pattern rather than a fixed text. Parentheses capture parts of the name, which the replacement puts back with `$1`, `$2`…, in any order.
Like Replace, it never touches the extension. While a pattern is being typed and is not valid yet, the step is marked ⚠ and changes nothing.

data.name: Regex_Pattern_Text
Regex_With_Text
data.value: The new text. `$1` puts back the first group, `$2` the second… Empty, it deletes what the pattern finds.

data.value: Checked, `[a-z]` finds lowercase letters only. Unchecked, case is ignored.

data.name: Regex_Example_Spaces

data.name: Case_Intro
data.value:
Changes uppercase and lowercase letters in the name. The extension is never touched: the **Extension** module does that.
A word is a run of letters, digits and apostrophes. Everything else separates words: spaces, dots, dashes, underscores… So `speedy.01x03.my_first-race` becomes `Speedy.01x03.My_First-Race` in Title case.

data.name: Case_Mode_Text
data.value: **lowercase**, **UPPERCASE**, **Title** (each word starts with a capital) or **Sentence** (only the first word does).

data.name: Case_SmallWords_Text
data.value: In Title case, these short words stay in lowercase, except at the start and at the end of the name, and at the start of a title within the name (after ` - `, `:`, `(`, `[` or an episode code such as `1x01`): `of`, `the`, `and`… in English, `de`, `la`, `et`… in French. In French, the word after `l'` or `d'` gets its capital: `de l'Épisode`.

data.name: Case_Exceptions_Text
data.value: Words always written as typed here, in every mode: `TV, iPhone, DVD`. Separated by commas.

data.name: Case_Roman_Text
data.value: In Title and Sentence case, `iv` or `xii` become `IV` and `XII`. Up to XXXIX only, so that ordinary words like “mix” or “civil” are left alone.

data.name: Case_Acronyms_Text
data.value: In Title and Sentence case, a word already written in uppercase (`DVD`, `USA`) stays so. Not when the whole name is in uppercase: `THE MATRIX` does become `The Matrix`.

data.name: Case_SpaceBeforeCapitals_Text
data.value: First puts a space between a lowercase letter and the capital that follows it, to separate words written together.

data.name: Remove_Intro
data.value:
Removes part of the name: a number of characters, a range of positions, or what is around a text. The extension is never touched.
Removing often leaves double spaces or a space before the extension: a **Clean** step at the end of the chain tidies them.

data.name: Numbering_Intro

Numbers the files and inserts the number in the name. The files are numbered **in their order**, the one of the grid: put a **Sort** step before this one, natural or by hand.
Unchecked files of the step are skipped, and do not use a number: the others are numbered 1, 2, 3 without gaps.

data.name: Extension_Intro
data.value:
Changes the extension, what follows the last dot: `.jpg`, `.mkv`. It is the only module that touches it; the others always leave it alone.
With **replace by** and **add after it**, the extension can be typed with or without its dot.

data.name: Filter_Intro
data.value:
Keeps the files that meet one criterion, or removes them. The files left out stay as they are on the disk, and the following steps no longer see them: a Numbering after a Filter numbers the files kept only, from 1.
One step tests one criterion. To combine several (the `.mkv` files of more than 1 GB), put several Filter steps one after the other: each one works on what the previous ones kept.
A filter with nothing to test (no text, no limit) keeps every file. In the grid of the step, the files left out are struck through.

data.name: FilterMode_Keep_Text
data.value: Keeps only the files that meet the criterion.

data.name: FilterMode_Remove_Text
data.value: Removes the files that meet the criterion, and keeps the others.

data.name: FilterOn_Name_Text
data.value: The current name, extension included, as the previous steps made it: **contains**, **starts with**, **ends with** a text, or matches a pattern or a regular expression.

data.name: TextTest_Wildcard_Text
data.value: The pattern covers the whole name: `*` stands for any text, `?` for one character. `*.mkv` keeps `a.mkv` but not `a.mkv.part`. Several patterns are separated by `;`: `*.mkv;*.mp4`.

data.name: TextTest_Regex_Text
data.value: A .NET regular expression, searched in the name: `S\d+E\d+` keeps the names with an episode number. A wrong expression shows in red on the step, which then keeps every file.

data.name: FilterOn_Extension_Text
data.value: A list of extensions separated by commas, with or without their dot, case ignored: `mkv, mp4`.

data.name: FilterOn_Size_Text
data.value: The size of the file, between two limits, in bytes, KB, MB or GB (1 KB = 1024 bytes). An empty box sets no limit on that side.

data.name: FilterOn_Modified_Text
data.value: The day the file was last modified, as shown by Explorer, from a day to another, both included. An empty box sets no limit on that side.

data.name: FilterOn_Length_Text
data.value: The number of characters of the current name, extension included. Useful to find the names too long for a device.

data.name: Filter_MatchCase_Text
data.value: For the name only. Checked, `VOSTFR` does not find `vostfr`.

data.name: Filter_Example_Contains
data.value: Keep the files whose name contains `VOSTFR`

data.name: Filter_Example_Wildcard
data.value: Keep the videos: pattern `*.mkv;*.mp4`

data.name: Filter_Example_Remove
data.value: Remove the extensions `nfo, txt`

data.name: Filter_Example_Regex
data.value: Keep the episodes: regular expression `\bS\d+E\d+\b`

data.name: PadNumbers_Intro
data.value:
Pads the numbers of the name with zeros: `Episode 5` → `Episode 05`, `S1E5` → `S01E05`. Without it, Explorer and many players list `Episode 10` before `Episode 2`.
A number is a run of digits from 0 to 9. A number already longer than asked is kept as it is. The extension is never touched: `Clip 7.3gp` → `Clip 07.3gp`.

data.value: Every number of the name. Careful with `x265` or `1080p`: they are numbers too, which only a number of digits larger than theirs changes.

data.name: ReplaceTable_Intro
data.value:
Replaces several texts at once, from a list: each line replaces a text by another, in the name without its extension. The lines apply in order, each on the result of the previous one.
A table is made to be reused: transliteration (`ß` → `ss`, `œ` → `oe`), the tags of your downloads (`VOSTFR` → `VOST`), your own vocabulary (`S01` → `Season 1`). Save it to a text file, then load it in another chain. Replace is simpler for one text; Replace (advanced) handles patterns.

data.value: Each line: the text to find and its replacement, empty to remove the text. Unchecked, the line stays in the table without being applied: handy to try without losing it.

data.name: ReplaceTable_Paste_Text
data.value: Adds the lines of the clipboard, one pair per line: the text and its replacement separated by a tab (two columns copied from a spreadsheet), `→`, `->` or `=`. A line without separator replaces its text by nothing.

data.name: ReplaceTable_Files_Text
data.value: **Load** adds the lines of a text file written the same way; **Save** writes the table to a file, one pair per line separated by a tab, which a spreadsheet opens as two columns.

data.value: Variables

data.name: Variables_Intro
data.value:
A variable is a word between braces that each file replaces by its own value: `{folder}` becomes the name of the file's folder, `{n}` its rank. Variables work in **Template**, **Insert**, and in the replacement text of **Replace** and **Replace (advanced)**.
Some take a format after a colon: `{n:3}` gives `007`, `{date:yyyyMMdd}` gives `20240517`. A **Capture** step adds its own variables, named as you wish, such as `{season}`. A word between braces that is not a variable stays as typed.

data.name: Variable_Name_Text
data.value: The current name, without its extension, as the previous steps made it.

data.name: Variable_Ext_Text
data.value: The extension, without its dot: `mkv`.

data.name: Variable_Folder_Text
data.value: The folder of the file: `Season 1`. `{folder:2}` is the folder above it (the series), `{folder:3}` the one above, and so on.

data.name: Variable_Number_Text
data.value: The rank of the file among those the step works on, from 1. `{n:3}` writes it on three digits: `001`. The Numbering module offers more (start, step, letters).

data.name: Variable_Date_Text
data.value: The date the file was last modified: `2024-05-17`. Any .NET date format after the colon: `{date:yyyy}` for the year, `{date:yyyy-MM-dd HH.mm}` with the time.

data.name: Variable_Today_Text
data.value: The date of the day, with the same formats as `{date}`.

data.name: Variable_Size_Text
data.value: The size of the file in the most readable unit: `1.5 MB`. `{size:KB}`, `{size:MB}` or `{size:GB}` give a rounded number in that unit, `{size:B}` the bytes.

data.name: Variable_Captured_Text
data.value: The variables of a Capture step placed earlier in the chain: `{season}`, `{episode}`… A number after the colon pads them with zeros: `{season:2}` gives `01`. They win over a built-in variable of the same name.

data.name: Variable_Captured_Label
data.value: Captured variables

data.name: Template_Intro
data.value:
Replaces the whole name, without its extension, by a template: some text and **variables** (see that page), which each file replaces by its own values. The extension is kept.
An empty template leaves the names as they are. Where a Template rebuilds the name entirely, Insert adds to it.

data.name: Template_Text_Text
data.value: The new name: text and variables. **Insert a variable** adds one at the end of the template.

data.name: Template_Example_Folders
data.value: `{folder:2} - {folder} - {n:2}`: the series, the season, the rank

data.name: Template_Example_Date
data.value: `{n:3} - {name}`: the rank in front of the name

data.name: Insert_Variables_Text
data.value: The text may hold **variables**: `[{folder}] ` puts the name of the folder in front of each file.

data.name: Insert_Example_Variable
data.value: The folder in front: `[{folder}] `

data.name: Capture_Intro
data.value:
Captures parts of the name into **variables**, without changing the name: a regular expression whose groups have a name, `(?<season>\d+)`, creates a variable of that name, `{season}`, that the following steps use in a Template, an Insert, a Replace, or to start a Numbering again.
To move a part of the name, capture it, remove it, then insert its variable elsewhere. In the grid of a Capture step, the after column shows the values captured from each name. A name the expression does not match gets no variable: `{season}` then stays as typed in its new name, which shows it at once.

data.name: Capture_Pattern_Text
data.value: A .NET regular expression, searched in the name without its extension. Each group written `(?<name>…)` creates `{name}`; plain groups `(…)` create nothing. Names ignore case: `{Season}` and `{season}` are the same.

data.name: Capture_MatchCase_Text
data.value: Checked, `x` does not find `X`.

data.name: Capture_Example_Template
data.value: Capture `(?<season>\d+)x(?<episode>\d+)`, then a Template `S{season}E{episode}`

data.name: Numbering_ResetOn_Text
data.value: A counter for each value of a variable: `season` (or `{season}`), captured earlier, numbers the episodes season by season. A template works too: `{date:yyyy}` starts again each year. The files of a value are numbered in the order of the list, even when other files come between them.

data.name: Numbering_Example_ResetOn
data.value: A counter per season: Capture `S(?<season>\d+)`, then For each value of `season`

data.name: Dates_Intro
data.value:
Finds the dates of the name and writes them in another format. Written year first, `2024-05-17`, dates sort in the order of time, which `17.05.2024` does not.
A date is three numbers separated by the same character (`.`, `-`, `_` or a space), or eight digits in a row (`20240517`). The year has two or four digits: `24` is 2024, `85` is 1985. What is not a real date, such as `31.02.2024` or a version number `1.2.3`, is left as it is. The extension is never touched.

data.name: Dates_Order_Text
data.value: How the dates are written in the names: day first in most of Europe, month first in the United States, year first for cameras and phones (`IMG_20240517`). `05.04.2024` is the 5th of April or the 4th of May depending on this choice.

data.name: Dates_Format_Text
data.value: The new format, as in .NET: `yyyy` the year, `MM` the month, `dd` the day, `MMMM` the name of the month, `dddd` that of the day, in the language of Windows. The panel shows what the format gives for May 17th, 2024.

data.name: Dates_Example_Iso
data.value: Day first, written year first

data.name: Dates_Example_Camera
data.value: A camera's date, `yyyyMMdd`, to `yyyy-MM-dd`

data.name: Dates_Example_Year
data.value: Only the year: format `yyyy`

data.name: List_Intro
data.value:
Renames from a list of lines: episode titles copied from a website, a track list, names prepared in a spreadsheet. Paste the list, type it, load a text file, or drop the file on the panel.
Line N goes to file N, in the order the files have at this step: put a **Sort** step just before, and compare the number of lines shown under the list with the number of files. An empty line keeps the name of its file, and so do the files beyond the last line. The lines may hold **variables**: `{n:2} - The First Lap`.

data.name: ListMode_ReplaceName_Text
data.value: The line replaces the name; the extension is kept.

data.name: ListMode_Insert_Text
data.value: The line is inserted in the name, where Insert would put it: at the start, at the end, at a position, before or after a text.

data.name: ListMode_Pairs_Text
data.value: Each line holds an old name and a new one, separated by a tab (two columns of a spreadsheet), `→` or `=`. The file is found by its name, not by its rank: the order does not matter. Written with its extension, the old name gives the whole new name; without, the extension is kept.

data.name: List_MatchCase_Text
data.value: Insert mode: for the text before or after which the line goes. Pairs mode: checked, `speedy 01` does not find `Speedy 01.mkv`.

data.name: List_Example_Titles
data.value: Episode titles, one per line

data.name: List_Example_Insert
data.value: Inserted at the end: ` - The First Lap`, ` - Rain on the Track`

data.name: List_Example_Pairs
data.value: Pairs: `Speedy 02 → Finale`, `Speedy 01 → Pilot`
